old: Protected-area evaluations often treat legal designation as a stable intervention, although practical authority can change while boundaries remain fixed. We examined whether Upemba National Park’s legal boundary remained aligned with disturbance under fragmented, militia-centred, and park-centred territorial-control profiles. We reconstructed the chronology before inspecting satellite outcomes, then measured recurrent fire and first crossings of tree-cover-loss and agricultural-expansion thresholds in 500 m cells from 2001 to 2022. Within environmental and accessibility strata, we estimated profile-specific inside–outside contrasts and compared the legal boundary with ten outward pseudo-boundaries.
new: Protected-area evaluations often treat legal designation as a stable intervention, although practical authority can change while boundaries remain fixed. We examined whether Upemba National Park’s legal boundary aligned with disturbance under fragmented, militia-centred, and park-centred territorial-control profiles. We combined a historical chronology with recurrent fire and first tree-cover-loss and agricultural-expansion threshold crossings in 500 m cells during 2001–2022. We estimated profile-specific inside–outside contrasts within landscape groups and compared the legal boundary with ten outward pseudo-boundaries.

old: At the primary 25% cumulative-loss threshold, tree-cover-loss odds were 57–76% lower inside under all profiles; pairwise profile differences remained uncertain. Legal-boundary estimates were more negative than all evaluated outward-offset estimates under every profile. In the better-balanced 5 km corridor, all point estimates remained negative, but only the park-centred interval excluded zero; estimates attenuated at the sparse 50% threshold. Fire contrasts varied among profiles in the primary model, yet comparable contrasts and sign reversals occurred at outward offsets. Agricultural-expansion estimates were inconclusive.
new: At the primary threshold, tree-cover-loss odds were 57–76% lower inside under all profiles; pairwise profile differences remained uncertain. Legal-boundary estimates were more negative than all evaluated outward estimates. This result weakened in the better-balanced 5 km corridor and at the sparse 50% threshold. Fire contrasts were higher under fragmented than militia-centred or park-centred control, but comparable contrasts and sign reversals occurred away from the legal line. Agricultural first-expansion estimates remained sensitive to the analysis period, persistence definition and uncertainty calculation.

old: The legal-boundary-aligned tree-cover-loss pattern across contrasting authority profiles demonstrates environmental equifinality: a favourable land-surface outcome does not identify the actor, mechanism, conservation intent, or legitimacy that produced it. Historical reconstruction, process-specific satellite observations, and pseudo-boundary diagnostics therefore answer distinct inferential questions and should remain analytically separate when protected-area authority changes over time.
new: A favourable land-surface outcome did not identify the actor, mechanism, conservation intent or legitimacy that produced it. Historical reconstruction, process-specific satellite observations and boundary-location diagnostics therefore answer distinct questions when protected-area authority changes over time. The estimates describe conditional spatial associations rather than causal effects of legal protection.

old: Protected areas are commonly evaluated as legal interventions that alter land use inside fixed boundaries. Studies often report lower habitat loss, anthropogenic pressure, or biodiversity decline inside than in comparable unprotected land (Andam et al., 2008; Geldmann et al., 2013, 2019; Gray et al., 2016; McNicol et al., 2023). Yet designation is not a stable intervention when the actors able to regulate access change. Protected areas territorialise space by defining rules and authorised actors, but these projects remain contested and historically variable (Bassett and Gautier, 2014; Holmes, 2014). We therefore treat protected-area boundaries as historically contingent territorial institutions whose environmental expression must be interpreted in relation to practical authority and disturbance process.
new: Legal designation establishes jurisdiction: it defines a protected area’s boundary and formal rules. Practical authority concerns who can implement or contest those rules. Protected areas are commonly evaluated by comparing environmental conditions inside and outside their boundaries, often finding lower habitat loss or pressure inside (Andam et al., 2008; Geldmann et al., 2013, 2019; Gray et al., 2016; McNicol et al., 2023). Yet the capacity to regulate access can change while the legal line remains fixed. Protected areas territorialise space through rules and authorised actors, but these institutions remain contested and historically variable (Bassett and Gautier, 2014; Holmes, 2014). Their environmental expression therefore requires evidence about practical authority as well as legal jurisdiction.

old: Agricultural expansion used the Annual Cropland Extent Dataset for Africa (Lou et al., 2025). An event was the first annual transition from below to at least 25% cropland, after which the cell left the risk set. The measure records first detected establishment at 500 m, not persistence, abandonment, or relocation (Table S16).
new: Agricultural expansion used the Annual Cropland Extent Dataset for Africa (Lou et al., 2025). An event was the first observed transition from below to at least 25% cropland, after which the cell left the risk set. Baseline agricultural cells were retained, so a subsequent decline and recrossing could define their first detected expansion within the observation window. This is not first-ever cultivation. We reconstructed annual 2000–2022 cropland fractions and verified every first-crossing date against the primary input. These observations support separate persistence, reversal and annual-presence analyses (Supplementary Methods S7; Tables S18–S20). None measures net agricultural change.

old: We varied event threshold (10%, 25%, 50%), spatial domain (5, 10, 20 km and full domain), and weighting. Exploratory chronology diagnostics shifted plausible transition years or omitted one episode. For sparse outcomes these diagnostics used the complete domain and an earlier implementation; only sign changes are comparable with the primary model. They assess dating uncertainty, not multi-year response lags. We also audited 2021–2022 fire harmonisation and applied strict beta-binomial fit criteria (Supplementary Methods S4; Tables S10–S13).
new: We varied event threshold (10%, 25%, 50%), spatial domain (5, 10, 20 km and full domain), and weighting. We distinguished the earlier exploratory chronology checks (Table S12) from the recovered, matched primary-corridor analyses of one- and two-year profile lags and transition-year exclusions (Supplementary Methods S5; Table S21). These assess temporal alignment, with altered eligible years; they do not identify delayed causal effects. Fire harmonisation and optimizer checks are reported in Supplementary Methods S3–S4 and Table S13. The retained 10% and 25% BFGS fits meet strict numerical criteria; the 50% fit does not meet the independent-gradient criterion.

old: Agricultural-expansion estimates were inconclusive. The primary park-centred contrast was negative and the other point estimates weakly positive, but weighting, threshold, domain, sparse events, and unstable offsets changed the inference (Fig. 3; Tables S8–S11, S14, S17).
new: The primary agricultural model retained 518 events (254 inside, 264 outside). Cell IDs, coordinates, sides, dates and corridor flags agreed between the primary input and post-event classifications. Restriction to 2001–2019 retained 442 first crossings, and corrected persistence retained 414 qualifying establishments. The park-centred contrast changed from −0.347 [−0.657, −0.037] in the full-period first-crossing model to −0.240 [−0.611, 0.131] in its restricted refit, then to −0.235 [−0.753, 0.284] under corrected persistence (Table S18). Shortening the period explained most of the point-estimate shift. The persistence standard error increased; overlapping intervals do not establish equivalent effects. The superseded 431-event estimate, −0.237 [−0.642, 0.168], used incomplete follow-up and is not the corrected result.

old: Figure 3. Primary pooled inside–outside contrasts within the symmetric 10 km corridor at the 25% threshold. (A) Profile-specific log-odds contrasts. (B) Pairwise differences. Points are estimates and bars are 95% conditional model-based confidence intervals; positive values indicate higher disturbance inside. Fire uses the beta-binomial model; tree-cover loss and agriculture use inverse-variance-weighted two-stage models with HC3 covariance. Intervals do not account for all spatial or serial dependence.
new: Figure 3. Primary pooled contrasts at the 25% threshold within the symmetric 10 km corridor. Panel A shows profile-specific inside-minus-outside log odds: positive values indicate higher disturbance inside, negative values lower disturbance inside. Panel B shows the first named profile’s contrast minus the second named profile’s contrast: positive values mean the contrast is more positive under the first profile, not necessarily higher disturbance inside. Bars are 95% conditional intervals calculated from the fitted covariance: SE(Lβ) = √(LΣLᵀ), including covariance between coefficients. They are not differences between interval endpoints. Fire uses a beta-binomial model; sparse outcomes use weighted two-stage models and HC3 covariance. Unresolved pairwise differences do not establish equivalence. Primary intervals do not account for all spatial or temporal dependence.
